video_title: How to Play Split Comps in Overwatch (Toronto vs Washington)
claim: A split composition can form two or sometimes three cores, creating pressure from distinct map areas rather than moving as a five-player rush unit.
review_note: General explanation; visual only needed for exact map geometry.

video_title: How to Play Split Comps in Overwatch (Toronto vs Washington)
claim: He calls the larger or tank-containing group the core and the smaller or tankless group the off angle, while acknowledging the terminology is partly conventional.
review_note: Preserve this local vocabulary rather than assume universal terms.

video_title: How to Play Split Comps in Overwatch (Toronto vs Washington)
claim: When one split core is rushed, it should retreat while the other pressures the enemy's trailing support and forces cooldowns, kills, or objective value; the two cores push and pull simultaneously.
review_note: Spoken mechanism clear; actual flank geometry and results require video review.

video_title: How to Play Split Comps in Overwatch (Toronto vs Washington)
claim: A pressured off angle has already contributed by drawing resources; trying to push both cores at once can throw away the advantage. The pressured core should keep attention while surviving.
review_note: He narrates a specific fight; do not treat outcome as independently verified.

claim: A turn is a period when a team spends cooldowns or takes space for proactive value; taking a first turn, a second turn, and a simultaneous neutralizing turn are distinct choices.
scope: Brawl and dive examples; poke acknowledged as less obvious
review_note: Explicit definition; transcript has automatic-caption errors for hero names elsewhere.

claim: Simultaneous neutralization tends to preserve the current map state, while sequential turns seek to change it. A team attacking a strong defensive setup cannot rely on neutralization alone to gain space.
review_note: Generalization as expressed by speaker, not proof across all maps.

claim: A space-poor dive team can pressure cart or set DPS angles to make the opposing Winston spend his first turn, creating a later second-turn opportunity.
review_note: Exact positioning depends on the on-screen demonstration.

claim: Soft dives can extend one's own time in while baiting enemy cooldown cycles; after the opposing Winston leaves, the team can use its second turn with backline and DPS aggression.
review_note: Specific execution sequence should be visually audited.

claim: A backline that follows its tank tightly around a corner is easier for the opposing tank to reach than a backline offset from that corner.
review_note: Requires visual review for geometry and example validity.

claim: He frames many Overwatch 2 fights as tank–backline reach and trade problems and says a team may engage or bait that interaction; these are broad explanatory simplifications, not strict composition taxonomy.
review_note: Potential tension with older brawl/dive/poke vocabulary, not a proved contradiction.

claim: A team going first around a corner can still plan to kite in the midfight; its backline needs an offset position and a window, such as an opponent's key cooldown being spent.
review_note: Map and cooldown names in ASR are unreliable; inspect original video.

claim: After a successful Genji engage, the player should recheck enemy threats before chasing another kill; tunnel vision turns a favorable trade into a needless coin flip.
review_note: Specific fight result is the speaker's interpretation.

claim: For Genji, tracking who is looking at him and when pressure shifts matters more than merely minimizing damage taken.
review_note: Strong phrasing depends on replay scene; preserve as his heuristic.

claim: He defines going first as choosing the engage and going second or baiting as allowing the opponent to commit before responding; hero and meta affect how those actions look.
review_note: Compare later refinements of first/second terminology.

claim: An effective bait setup preserves the ability to punish an incoming engage; simply kiting without ever standing ground to punish it misses the purpose.
review_note: Video needed to test whether the setup actually prevented the engage.

video_title: Why do Dives Always Kill You
claim: The expected outcome of a mirrored Winston–Tracer dive depends heavily on the quality of each dive's staging, rather than a fixed rule that the backline always lives or dies.
review_note: Speaker recognizes player skill and ultimates as additional factors.

video_title: Why do Dives Always Kill You
claim: Against a well-staged dive, reviewing only defensive cooldown execution is often too late; instead, prevent the Tracer angle or Winston jump from becoming favorable before walking up.
review_note: The emphatic 'impossible to live' rhetoric is conditional on a genuinely good dive.

video_title: Why do Dives Always Kill You
claim: A wide retake route can clear or displace the dive setup, presenting the enemy Winston with a poor long-distance dive or a concession of space.
review_note: Requires map and POV review before elevating to a general rule.

video_title: How to SEE Overwatch Like GEEKAY Esports
claim: Before a good setup, teammates should maximize safe sight of the enemy; he distinguishes broad team sight from scouting a specific player.
review_note: His term 'sight maxing' is local vocabulary, not a validated metric.

video_title: How to SEE Overwatch Like GEEKAY Esports
claim: Poking far forward between fights can reveal the enemy's walk-up, after which a team can withdraw behind a corner while retaining information and denying the same view to its opponent.
review_note: Visual inspection needed to verify visibility for each POV.

claim: The pre-fight staging phase is a contest over how each team shapes the fight; conceding angles and retreating only after the enemy has finished setting up can lose before the nominal engage.
review_note: Avoid turning regional rhetoric into a universal empirical claim.

video_title: Why Good Players Make Stupid Mistakes
claim: Replay analysis should reconstruct what players could know and were prioritizing at the moment, rather than explain a death solely with hindsight.
review_note: Ascribes possible mental states; verify through player POV where possible.

video_title: Why Good Players Make Stupid Mistakes
claim: A postgame list of correct actions can be less useful than identifying the in-game attention process that prevented known actions from being executed under limited mental bandwidth.
review_note: Distinct from denying value of tactical knowledge.

video_title: How To Win Without Doing Damage
claim: Low-damage double-flex DPS setups cannot rely as much on forcing tank cooldowns or long-range picks; they depend more on pathing, scouting, and avoiding head-on contests.
review_note: Patch and composition context must be checked before generalizing.

video_title: How To Win Without Doing Damage
claim: A DPS may yield an angle to an opponent's clearing attempt, preserving own resources; the opponent's spent movement and subsequent retreat become a window to re-enter.
review_note: Counterplay depends on exact paths and cooldown state.

claim: Ultimate economy still exists, but he argues it generally carries less explanatory weight in Overwatch 2 than in Overwatch 1; he explicitly exempts some D.Va, Zarya, and Symmetra compositions.
review_note: Title is deliberately stronger than the actual spoken claim.

claim: More individual playmaking, splits, and messy trades can let a team win despite spending or facing an apparent ultimate deficit.
review_note: Match outcome examples have not been independently checked.

claim: Spacing the backline while a sturdier front line shows can draw an enemy ultimate and permit a kite, making the opponent's stored ultimate less decisive.
scope: Specific bait example; more mobile OW2 context
review_note: Visual review required for the actual spacing and timing.

claim: Winning a fight can generate later ultimate charge and next-fight setup; losing a fight creates a retake burden, so counting only ultimates spent omits these state changes.
review_note: Numerical charge examples should be checked visually.

claim: When a direct push through a prepared Sig/Bastion and Mei defense is unworkable, backing out early can hide a new route and create a later push opportunity.
review_note: Do not generalize as retreating whenever pushing is hard.

claim: Early voluntary withdrawal while cooldowns and distance remain differs from backing up after poke has forced a retreat; the latter can allow pursuit and further loss of space.
scope: Explicit response to possible tension with prior 'Lock Eyes and Fight' video
review_note: Speaker himself flags and reconciles the apparent contradiction.

claim: After spending an unsuccessful first turn, a team can retreat before the opponent closes, retain room to act, and regain the initiative for a later turn.
review_note: Outcome and spacing need visual verification.

video_title: Playing Second: The Mind Control Warfare of Team Falcons
claim: First and second are useful descriptions of timing but poor instructions on their own; playing second requires flexible coverage of possible opponent decisions.
review_note: Refines the 2023–2024 vocabulary without rejecting it.

video_title: Playing Second: The Mind Control Warfare of Team Falcons
claim: A team seeking to play second may intentionally offer a cooldown trade or punishable position to induce a predictable opponent commitment, then arrange a counter-engage.
review_note: Speaker also shows this can fail; see P4-035.

video_title: Playing Second: The Mind Control Warfare of Team Falcons
claim: The first-moving team can accept such bait if it responds quickly and coherently; a second-moving team that spends cooldowns to bait and then merely mirrors the same engage risks losing the cooldown trade.
review_note: Prevents treating P4-034 as an always-win rule.

claim: In the later follow-up he maintains that spending multiple support ultimates to win can be acceptable; the reviewed failure was spending them while losing and without a viable post-fight setup.
review_note: Explicitly distinguishes ult spending from failure to win a fight.

claim: In the reviewed Zenyatta–Brigitte fight, he prefers a wide swing and kiting the opposing response rather than committing into it with both support ultimates.
scope: Specific match, may depend on cooldown tracking
review_note: He acknowledges uncertainty about exact ult tracking.

claim: A point flip is insufficient if the team clusters on point and lacks angles or a pinch for the next touch; the quality of the resulting setup matters more than the count of ultimates spent.
review_note: Visually validate positioning and outcome.

claim: Poking past a choke before backing up can locate the opponent and preserve initiative; simply holding the choke can permit the enemy to arrange its own play.
review_note: Short clip; not enough context for a universal rule.

claim: For players below the highest level, he recommends deliberate observation of real games over relying on first-principles mental simulation of an extremely complex game.
scope: 2026-09 learning advice; explicitly qualified for top experts
review_note: Rhetorical ranking advice, not a measured learning experiment.

claim: He recommends writing a detailed record of a pro replay to expose unnoticed events and patterns, then comparing a closely matched own replay to identify differences.
review_note: He admits the three-step scheme was improvised; do not invent a missing step.

claim: When testing a tactical disagreement, seek several closely comparable real examples and check for confounds rather than relying only on hypothetical arguments.
review_note: Consistent with P4-022 but a distinct claim about evidence.
